Running a grid on a cloud VM

Source: vignettes/articles/grid-on-a-vm.Rmd
grid-on-a-vm.Rmd

A recovery grid fits one model per cell, and the cells do not depend on each other. On a laptop they run one after another, each on as many cores as it has chains. A cloud virtual machine with 32 or 64 cores can run several cells at once. This article shows how to split one recovery_grid() call over several R processes on one such machine, with the launcher that ships with bmmtools. Nothing here needs a batch scheduler. The same R side works under one, and a sketch for SLURM is at the end.

The split changes where cells run, not what they are. Every cell keeps the seed and the file names that one sequential run would give it. The processes together therefore write the cells that a single call writes, and collect_grid() reads them as one grid.

How a split run works

A split run has three steps, all in one grid directory:

  1. The setup call is your recovery_grid() call with cells = integer(0). It runs once. It writes grid.rds, runs the preflight fit, fits the priors of prior_sd if you asked for them, and simulates the data of every cell. It fits no cell.
  2. The slices are the same call, each with cells = grid_tasks(grid, reps, n)[[k]], one per process. grid_tasks() cuts the cells into n runs of consecutive cells. Each slice first checks that its call matches the one the setup call recorded, then fits its own cells. The check covers the design, the seed, the prior, the model and formula, and the fitter’s arguments. A slice of another grid stops before it fits anything.
  3. Collecting. collect_grid(dir) reads every cell’s results from its files. attr(x, "run_info") has one row per call that reached its cells: which cells it ran, for how many it found results from an earlier run, how many failed, when it started and ended, and the machine and package versions. A call that stopped with an error before its first fit leaves no row.
args <- list(
  model = bmm::mixture2p(resp_error = "y"),
  grid = expand.grid(n_subjects = c(20, 50), n_trials = c(30, 100)),
  pars = c(kappa = log(8), thetat = qlogis(0.75)),
  sds = c(kappa = 0.3, thetat = 0.5),
  dir = "fits/mixture2p", reps = 10, seed = 1,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, backend = "cmdstanr"
)

# once
do.call(recovery_grid, c(args, list(cells = integer(0))))

# in process k of 4
tasks <- grid_tasks(args$grid, args$reps, 4)
do.call(recovery_grid, c(args, list(cells = tasks[[k]])))

# afterwards, here or on another machine
out <- collect_grid("fits/mixture2p")
summary(out)
attr(out, "run_info")

Run each slice in its own R process. A parallel backend inside one session can change the random number generator its workers use, and then the fits differ from a sequential run. The launcher below starts one Rscript per slice.

The launcher

bmmtools ships three files for this, which you copy and edit:

file.copy(
  system.file("templates", "vm", package = "bmmtools"), ".",
  recursive = TRUE
)
  • vm/grid-args.R is your grid, written once as a list called grid_args: everything you would pass to recovery_grid() except cells. Every process reads this file, so the setup call and the slices cannot drift apart.
  • vm/grid-slice.R runs the setup call (setup) or one slice (<k> <n>). You can run it by hand.
  • vm/launch.sh runs the setup call and then starts the slices. It also reports on them and restarts one.

From the directory that dir in grid-args.R is relative to:

bash vm/launch.sh vm/grid-args.R

The launcher reads the machine’s cores and the cores one slice uses: its chains, times the threads of each chain. It starts as many slices as fit, so 32 cores and 4 chains give 8 slices. -k sets the number yourself. The launcher refuses a number that would put more chains than cores on the machine unless you add --force.

The setup call runs in the foreground and logs to <dir>/logs/setup.log. If it fails, nothing else starts, and stopping the launcher stops the setup call too. It also stops when the SSH session ends, and simulating a large grid can take a while, so start the launcher inside tmux or screen. The slices run in the background under nohup, so they go on after the SSH session ends. Each one writes <dir>/logs/slice-<k>.log, which ends with a line EXIT <status> when the process finishes: EXIT 0 when every cell has a fit, EXIT 1 when some failed. To see how far they are:

bash vm/launch.sh --status vm/grid-args.R

--status prints the state of the setup call, the number of cells with a result and, for each slice, its exit line, running with its process id, or stopped without an exit line for a process that is gone without one (the machine restarted, or something killed it hard). A recorded process id that another process has taken since, as after a restart or by a slice of another grid, does not count as running. This needs a working ps, as does stopping every process a slice’s R started (below). Without one the launcher says so: it then counts a slice as running while a process group with its recorded id is live, and the setup call while a process with its recorded id is. A kill of a slice still stops its R and the processes R started in the slice’s process group. Only processes in a session of their own survive it, such as the Stan chains that cmdstanr starts through processx.

The launcher runs one launch at a time. It refuses to start while another launch sets up or starts the same grid, and while a slice of its last launch still runs, so two launches do not fit the same cells at once. It cannot see slices that you start by hand.

To stop a slice, send its process id from <dir>/logs/pids a plain kill. The slice’s R process and the processes R started, such as the Stan chains, stop with it, and the log gets its exit line. A kill -9 stops only the process you name and leaves no exit line. Its R fits on, so --status still shows the slice as running, with a note that the process is gone and the kill command, with the ids of its R and of what R started, that stops the rest. Without a working ps the note gives kill -- -<id> instead, which stops the processes of the slice’s process group, its R among them, but not those in a session of their own. A kill -9 on the launcher during the setup call leaves the setup running: a new launch is refused until it ends, and no slices start from it. --status then shows the kill command that stops the setup and what it started. Without a working ps it names only the setup’s own process, and what the setup started in a session of its own outlives that kill.

If the slices die when you log out, the machine ends a user’s processes at logout (KillUserProcesses=yes in systemd’s logind.conf), which nohup does not prevent; check that setting first.

When a slice stops

A cell’s results are written the moment it finishes, each file under a temporary name first and then renamed. A slice that is killed leaves the cells it finished and nothing half-written. Start it again:

bash vm/launch.sh --rerun 3 vm/grid-args.R

This runs slice 3 of the last launch in the background, as the launcher first did, and does not repeat the setup call. The slice skips the cells that have results and fits the rest. A refitted cell draws the same chains it would have drawn the first time: a split run always has a seed.

Bringing the results home

The fits are large. The results are small. collect_grid() needs grid.rds, prior-sd.rds (if the grid has one), the run-info/ folder, and each cell’s -sim.rds and -est.rds files. It does not need the fits:

rsync -av --include='*/' --include='grid.rds' --include='prior-sd.rds' \
  --include='run-info/*' --include='*-sim.rds' --include='*-est.rds' \
  --exclude='*' vm:project/fits/mixture2p/ fits/mixture2p/

What to set up on the machine

The launcher installs nothing. The machine needs R, CmdStan with a C++ toolchain, and the versions of bmm, brms, cmdstanr and bmmtools you mean to report. Each process compiles the model once at its start. run_info() on the machine shows what is installed, and each slice’s record keeps it.

Leave cmdstanr_write_stan_file_dir unset, or give each process its own directory. Processes that start together and share one directory would compile the same executable at the same time.

Several machines

Run the setup call on one machine and copy the grid directory to the others. Install the same versions of bmmtools, bmm and brms on every machine: grid.rds records these three, and a slice on a machine with other versions of them stops. Keep R and CmdStan the same too. The check does not cover them, but each slice’s run record shows what it ran on. Then give each machine its share of the slices, for example slices 1–8 of 16 on the first and 9–16 on the second. The launcher always runs all of its slices, so here you start them by hand, one Rscript per slice, with the same total on every machine:

nohup Rscript vm/grid-slice.R vm/grid-args.R 9 16 > slice-9.log 2>&1 &

The slices write disjoint files as long as every machine splits the grid into the same 16. Copying the directories back into one gives the whole grid.

Under a batch scheduler

On a cluster with a scheduler, each array task runs one slice. A SLURM sketch:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --array=1-16
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
Rscript vm/grid-slice.R vm/grid-args.R "$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID" 16
echo "EXIT $?"

Run the setup call before you submit the array, on the login node or as a job of its own that the array waits for:

Rscript vm/grid-slice.R vm/grid-args.R setup

The run records fill in scheduler, job_id, array_task_id and cores_granted from the scheduler’s environment (SLURM, PBS, LSF or SGE).
